[CONFLICT] The claim that GDP fails to capture non-material dimensions of wellbeing is disputed because standard economic measures prioritize material output, while alternative frameworks (e.g., happiness indices, human development index) argue that health, social connections, and environmental quality are essential to wellbeing but are omitted from GDP calculations.

C005.subject: GDP per capita
C005.object: material living standards only when adjusted for income inequality and household net worth
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita material living standards only when adjusted for income inequality and household net worth]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Income Distribution Database (IDD) and OECD Wealth Distribution Database, cross-referenced with national accounts data for GDP per capita — Provides panel data on income inequality (e.g., Gini coefficients) and household net worth across OECD countries post-1950, enabling direct statistical tests of whether adjusting GDP per capita for these factors improves its correlation with direct measures of material living standards (e.g., consumption, housing quality).

[PATH:literature] Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Commission Report (2009) and subsequent literature on 'Beyond GDP' indicators — Offers theoretical and empirical arguments for the limitations of GDP per capita as a welfare proxy, and proposes alternative composite indices (e.g., the OECD Better Life Index). Reviewing this literature can identify established methodologies for incorporating inequality and wealth adjustments, and highlight empirical tests of their validity.

[PATH:empirical] Empirical replication study using the Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) and the Household Finance and Consumption Survey (HFCS) — Allows construction of a synthetic material living standards index (e.g., median disposable income adjusted for household net worth) and comparison with GDP per capita across OECD countries. Regression or correlation analyses can directly test whether inequality- and wealth-adjusted GDP per capita better tracks the synthetic index than unadjusted GDP per capita.

C006.subject: GDP per capita
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP per capita income inequality and non-market activities]

[PATH:literature] Piketty, T. (2014). Capital in the Twenty-First Century. Harvard University Press. — Provides empirical data on long-run income inequality trends across countries, directly testing whether GDP per capita growth masks distributional changes.

[PATH:empirical] World Bank World Development Indicators: Gini coefficient data paired with GDP per capita time series (1950–present) — Allows statistical comparison of GDP per capita growth with changes in income inequality globally, revealing periods where GDP per capita increases while inequality worsens.

[PATH:theoretical] Stiglitz, J., Sen, A., & Fitoussi, J.-P. (2009). Report by the Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress. — Provides a theoretical framework and empirical examples of how GDP per capita fails to capture non-market activities (e.g., unpaid care work, volunteerism) and why this omission biases economic output measures.

C007.subject: GDP growth
C007.object: subjective social connection scores in post-industrial economies
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth subjective social connection scores in post-industrial economies]

[PATH:empirical] World Values Survey (WVS) longitudinal data on subjective well-being and social connection, merged with national GDP growth rates from the World Bank (2000-2020) — Directly tests the hypothesized negative correlation across post-industrial economies using multi-country panel data, controlling for confounds like inequality or unemployment.

[PATH:literature] Review of Putnam's 'Bowling Alone' thesis and subsequent research on social capital decline in affluent nations (e.g., Robert Putnam, 2000; recent updates in American Journal of Sociology) — Provides theoretical grounding and historical evidence that economic growth in post-industrial contexts may erode community ties and subjective social connection, supporting the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies on the impact of local economic shocks (e.g., plant closures, booms) on social network density and perceived loneliness (e.g., using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel or UK Household Longitudinal Study) — Isolates causal mechanisms by examining how changes in GDP (or local income) affect individual-level social connection, helping to confirm or refute the direction of correlation.

qualifier.geographic: post-industrial economies (e.g., Western Europe, North America, Japan, Australia)

C008.subject: GDP
C008.object: key drivers of economic growth that can indirectly improve non-material dimensions of wellbeing
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP key drivers of economic growth that can indirectly improve non-material dimensions of wellbeing]

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and GDP panel data (2000-2020) — analyze correlations between GDP growth and non-material wellbeing indicators (e.g., life satisfaction, social connections, work-life balance) across OECD countries. — Directly tests whether GDP growth is associated with improvements in non-material dimensions of wellbeing, controlling for other factors, in the specified temporal and geographic scope.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox literature (Easterlin, 1974; updated studies post-2000) — review meta-analyses and longitudinal studies on the relationship between income growth and subjective wellbeing in developed economies. — Provides established theoretical and empirical evidence on whether GDP-driven growth translates into non-material wellbeing gains, challenging the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Endogenous growth theory and human capital models (e.g., Romer, Lucas) — examine mechanisms linking GDP drivers (e.g., innovation, education) to non-material outcomes (e.g., health, civic engagement) via spillover effects. — Offers a causal framework to explain how GDP growth might indirectly improve non-material wellbeing, supporting the hypothesis under specific conditions.

C009.subject: GDP growth
C009.object: subjective wellbeing in high-income contexts when income inequality rises above a Gini threshold of 0.35
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth subjective wellbeing in high-income contexts when income inequality rises above a Gini threshold of 0.35]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and European Social Survey (ESS) linked to national Gini coefficients and GDP growth rates for OECD countries post-2008 — Directly tests the conditional correlation between GDP growth and subjective wellbeing at varying inequality levels, allowing for threshold analysis around Gini = 0.35.

[PATH:literature] Re-analysis of Easterlin Paradox literature focusing on income inequality as a moderator (e.g., studies by Richard Easterlin, or recent meta-analyses in Journal of Happiness Studies) — Provides theoretical grounding and existing empirical evidence for the interaction between inequality and growth on wellbeing, helping to identify whether the proposed threshold holds across studies.

[PATH:theoretical] Behavioral economics experiments or survey-based studies on relative income and social comparisons in high-income contexts (e.g., Kahneman & Deaton's work on income and emotional wellbeing) — Explores the psychological mechanisms linking inequality to diminished wellbeing returns from growth, which could explain the hypothesized negative correlation above a Gini threshold.

C010.subject: GDP growth
C010.object: wellbeing indicators across all income contexts
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth wellbeing indicators across all income contexts]

[PATH:empirical] World Happiness Report (2000-2020) coupled with World Bank GDP per capita data — Cross-national panel data can test whether GDP growth rates correlate with subjective wellbeing (e.g., life satisfaction) across low-, middle-, and high-income countries, controlling for baseline income.

[PATH:literature] Easterlin Paradox meta-analysis (e.g., Easterlin et al., 2010; updated studies) — This body of research directly examines the relationship between economic growth and happiness, providing theoretical and empirical evidence on whether the correlation holds across all income contexts or diminishes beyond a threshold.

[PATH:empirical] OECD Better Life Index and Gallup World Poll data (2000-2020) — Multidimensional wellbeing indicators (health, education, social connections) can be regressed on GDP growth rates to assess whether the correlation is consistent across diverse income levels, addressing potential nonlinearities.
